title: Arguments that are not ours
source_text: Διόπερ μάτην λέλεκται τῷ Κέλσῳ, ὡς μὴ εἰδότι τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅτι ἐπείπερ πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ υἱὸς ἐν ἀνθρωπίνῳ γεγονὼς σώματι, οὐδ᾿ ἂν αὐτὸς εἴη ἀθάνατος ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ υἱός. εἶτα πάλιν ἑαυτῷ φύρει τὸν λόγον, ὥς τινων ἀφ᾿ ἡμῶν οὐχ ὁμολογησόντων πνεῦμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν ἀλλὰ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ, καὶ οἴεται ἀπαντᾶν λέγων ὅτι οὐδεμία τοιαύτη φύσις ἐστὶ πνεύματος, ὥστ᾿ ἀεὶ διαμένειν· ὡσεὶ καὶ, λεγόντων ἡμῶν ὅτι ὁ θεὸς „πῦρ“ ἐστι „καταναλίσκον,“ ἔλεγεν ὅτι οὐδεμία τοιαύτη φύσις ἐστὶ πυρὸς, ὥστ᾿ ἀεὶ διαμένειν· οὐχ ὁρῶν πῶς λέγομεν εἶναι „πῦρ“ τὸν θεὸν ἡμῶν, καὶ τίνων ἀναλωτικὸν, ὅτι ἁμαρτημάτων καὶ τῆς κακίας. πρέπει γὰρ θεῷ ἀγαθῷ μετὰ τὸ ἕκαστον φανῆναι ἀγωνισάμενον, ὁποῖος γέγονεν ἀγωνιστὴς, ἀναλῶσαι τῷ πυρὶ τῶν κολάσεων τὴν κακίαν. εἶτα πάλιν ἑαυτῷ τὸ μὴ λεγόμενον ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν λαμβάνει. ὅτι ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι τὸ ἀναπεπνευκέναι τὸν θεόν. καὶ τούτῳ ἀκόλουθον τὸ μὴ δύνασθαι ἀναστῆναι μετὰ τοῦ σώματος τὸν Ἰησοῦν· οὐκ ἂν γὰρ ἀπειλήφει ὃ δέδωκε πνεῦμα ὁ θεὸς καταμεμολυσμένον τῇ τοῦ σώματος φύσει. εὔηθες οὖν ἀπαντᾶν ἡμᾶς πρὸς τοὺς λόγους ὡς ἡμετέρους τοὺς μὴ ἡμετέρους.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore in vain (μάτην) it has been said by Celsus, as not knowing (οἶδα) the things of the Spirit of God, that since (ἐπείπερ) the Son is a spirit from God having come to be (γίνομαι) in a human (ἀνθρώπινος) body, not even the Son of God himself would be immortal (ἀθάνατος). Then again for himself he confuses/jumbles (φύρω) the argument (λόγος), as though some of us would not confess (ὁμολογέω) that God is spirit but his Son, and thinks to meet (ἀπαντάω) (it) saying that no such nature (φύσις) of spirit is, so as always to endure (διαμένω); as though also, when we say that God is 'a consuming fire', he were saying that no such nature of fire is, so as always to endure; not seeing how we say our God is 'fire', and of what things consuming (ἀναλωτικός), that (it is) of sins (ἁμάρτημα) and of wickedness (κακία). For it befits (πρέπει) a good (ἀγαθός) God, after each has been shown (φαίνομαι) having contended (ἀγωνίζομαι), of what sort a contender (ἀγωνιστής) he has become, to consume (ἀναλίσκω) with the fire of punishments (κόλασις) the wickedness. Then again for himself he takes (λαμβάνω) what is not said by us, that it is necessary (ἀναγκαῖον) for God to have breathed again/back (ἀναπνέω, pf. inf. ἀναπεπνευκέναι). And consequent (ἀκόλουθον) on this, that Jesus is not able to rise (ἀνίστημι) with the body; for God would not have received back (ἀπολαμβάνω) the spirit which he gave, defiled (καταμολύνω) by the nature of the body. Foolish (εὔηθες) then for us to meet arguments as ours which are not ours.
pass_b_english: So Celsus, as one who does not know the things of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14), has spoken to no purpose when he says: “Since the Son is a spirit from God that has come to be in a human body, not even the Son of God himself would be immortal.”

Then again he muddles the argument to suit himself, as though some of us would grant not that God is spirit but that his Son is, and he thinks he meets this by saying: “There is no spirit of such a nature that it lasts forever.” It is as if, when we say that God is “a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29), he were to say: “There is no fire of such a nature that it lasts forever.” He does not see in what sense we say that our God is “fire,” and what it is that he consumes: sins and wickedness. For it befits a good God, once it has become clear, after each one has contended, what kind of contender he has been, to consume wickedness with the fire of punishments.

Then again he assumes, to suit himself, something we do not say: “It is necessary that God drew his breath back in”; and, as following from this, that “Jesus could not rise with his body; for God would not have taken back the spirit he gave once it had been defiled by the nature of the body.” It is foolish, then, for us to answer arguments as if they were ours, when they are not ours.

choices.choice: Celsus’s arguments, introduced by ὅτι and reported as his, are put in double quotation marks; the Greek gives them in indirect form, so the wording is close to, not certainly identical with, Celsus’s own. ‘That has come to be in a human body’ renders ἐν ἀνθρωπίνῳ γεγονὼς σώματι. ὡς ... οὐχ ὁμολογησόντων πνεῦμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν ἀλλὰ τὸν υἱόν: rendered ‘as though some of us would grant not that God is spirit but that his Son is’. ἑαυτῷ φύρει / ἑαυτῷ ... λαμβάνει rendered ‘to suit himself’. ‘The things of the Spirit of God’ repeats 1 Corinthians 2:14, quoted in 6.71. ‘Consuming fire’: Hebrews 12:29 (also Deuteronomy 4:24, cited at 6.70). μετὰ τὸ ἕκαστον φανῆναι ἀγωνισάμενον, ὁποῖος γέγονεν ἀγωνιστής: φανῆναι is passive in sense, so ‘once it has become clear ... what kind of contender he has been’. ἀναπεπνευκέναι (perfect infinitive of ἀναπνέω) is doubtful: rendered ‘drew his breath back in’, which fits the next clause (God would not take back the spirit he gave); ‘breathed out’ is possible but fits the argument less well. τούτῳ ἀκόλουθον stays under ‘he assumes’: the consequence is Celsus’s, not Origen’s. κόλασις rendered ‘punishments’; Origen elsewhere gives such punishment a healing purpose, but the word here is left plain.
'born in a human body' to 'that has come to be in a human body' (γεγονώς, not γεννηθείς)
'muddles his own argument' to 'muddles the argument to suit himself' (ἑαυτῷ φύρει τὸν λόγον)
'would not agree that God is spirit, but only that his Son is' to 'would grant not that God is spirit but that his Son is' ('only' was added)
'once each one has shown in the contest what kind of contender' to 'once it has become clear, after each one has contended, what kind of contender' (φανῆναι is passive; agency fixed)
'he takes on his own' to 'he assumes, to suit himself' (ἑαυτῷ ... λαμβάνει)
'took his breath back again' to 'drew his breath back in' (avoids the idiom 'catch one's breath')
'And from this it follows that' to 'and, as following from this, that' (τούτῳ ἀκόλουθον stays inside what Celsus assumes, so Origen does not assert the inference)

choices.choice: 6.72: ἀναπεπνευκέναι ('drew his breath back in') is a doubtful reading. 'Breathed out' is also possible. It is flagged in translator_notes and is not a reason to hold the chunk.

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
